title: CPU Profiling
description: Learn to use Chrome DevTools CPU profiling to find slow functions, long tasks, and optimization opportunities in real applications.

data.text: CPU profiling records how your application spends its time. A profiler snapshots the call stack at regular intervals and produces a flame chart that reveals which functions consume the most CPU, which call paths are deep, and where long tasks are formed.

The DevTools Performance panel produces a flame chart of activity over time. Wide bars mean slow functions. Tall stacks mean deep call paths. Red bars indicate forced synchronous layouts. Bottom-Up and Call Tree views rank functions by self time, making it easy to spot the real bottlenecks.

data.title: Chrome DevTools CPU Profiling Steps
data.content: Capture and analyze a CPU profile.
data.code:
1. Open DevTools (F12) > Performance tab
2. Click the gear icon and enable:
   - Screenshots
   - Web Vitals
   - Advanced Paint Instrumentation (if needed)
3. Click Record (circle button)
4. Interact with the app: scroll, click, resize
5. Stop recording
6. Analyze:
   - Summary tab: overall activity breakdown
   - Bottom-Up: functions ranked by self time
   - Call Tree: hierarchical execution time
   - Event Log: timeline of events

Key indicators:
- Long yellow 'Scripting' blocks → JS work
- Long purple 'Rendering' blocks → layout/paint
- Red 'Layout (forced)' bars → forced reflow
- Tasks >50 ms → potential input-blocking

data.text: A long task is any JavaScript execution that blocks the main thread for more than 50 ms. Long tasks delay user input, animations, and page responsiveness. The Long Tasks API and DevTools both flag these events automatically.

data.title: Simulating and Observing Long Tasks

data.text: The flame chart is a time-based view. Each frame of execution is a stack of function calls. Wide stacks indicate functions that take a long time. Narrow stacks that appear many times indicate frequently called functions. Use the Bottom-Up view to find high self-time functions regardless of call path.

data.title: Flame Chart Reading Guide
data.content: How to read a DevTools flame chart.
data.code:
Flame Chart anatomy:

X axis: time
Y axis: call stack depth

Top-most bar = currently executing function
Bars below it = parent callers

Colors:
- Yellow = JavaScript execution
- Purple = rendering (layout/paint)
- Green = painting
- Red = forced layout
- Gray = other

Reading priority:
1. Find the longest yellow bar → likely a slow function
2. Check Bottom-Up for highest 'Self Time'
3. Check if it is called from many places (high 'Total Time')
4. Determine if the function can be optimized, cached, or split

data.text: DevTools CPU profiling uses sampling by default, which pauses execution briefly to record the call stack. Sampling has minimal overhead but may miss very short functions. Instrumentation records every function call and return with high accuracy but slows execution significantly.

data.title: Sampling Profiler Settings
data.content: Configure the profiler for different scenarios.
data.code:
CPU Profiler modes:

Sampling (default):
- Records stack every 1 ms (approximately)
- Low overhead (~1-5%)
- Good for long recordings
- May miss sub-millisecond functions

Instrumentation:
- Records every function call and return
- High overhead (5-10x slowdown)
- Good for micro-benchmarks
- Not suitable for long recordings

When to use each:
- Sampling: general performance audits, field recordings
- Instrumentation: comparing two implementations precisely

In DevTools:
- Performance panel → always uses sampling
- Profiles panel → supports both sampling and instrumentation

data.text: Focus profiling on known hotspots: data processing loops, render cycles, event handlers, third-party scripts, and large array operations. Measure before and after any optimization to confirm improvement.

data.title: Optimization Workflow with Profiling
data.code:
Profiling-driven optimization workflow:

1. Profile the baseline
   - Record Performance panel
   - Note total scripting time, long tasks
   - Identify top 3 functions by self time

2. Form a hypothesis
   - 'Map over 10k items in render'
   - 'Unmemoized callback recreates closures'
   - 'Third-party script runs on main thread'

3. Apply one change
   - Memoize with useMemo / useCallback
   - Virtualize list
   - Move work to Web Worker

4. Profile again
   - Same scenario, same device
   - Compare scripting time and task count

5. Validate with field metrics
   - INP / FID from CrUX or web-vitals library
   - Confirm user-facing improvement

data.title: Optimizations Can Be Reverted
data.text: Always profile before optimizing and compare after. Your intuition about what is slow is often wrong. Some optimizations hurt more than they help. Measure everything.

terms.definition: A time-based visualization of function call stacks, where width indicates duration.
Any main-thread JavaScript execution blocking the browser for more than 50 ms.
Time spent executing a function itself, excluding time in child functions.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CPU profiling records function execution time and call stacks
Flame charts visualize time on the x-axis and call depth on the y-axis
Wide bars indicate slow functions; tall stacks indicate deep call paths
Long tasks are >50 ms of main-thread JavaScript and harm interactivity
Use Bottom-Up view to find functions with highest self time
Always profile before and after to confirm optimization impact
Sampling profilers are low-overhead and suitable for long recordings
data.takeaway: CPU profiling turns guesswork into evidence. Focus on the hottest functions, measure changes, and validate with real-world metrics like INP.
